data.title: There's A Lot To Like About Eldorado Gold's (TSE:ELD) Upcoming US$0.075 Dividend
data.description:
Regular readers will know that we love our dividends at Simply Wall St, which is why it's exciting to see Eldorado Gold Corporation (TSE:ELD) is about to trade ex-dividend in the next three days. The ex-dividend date occurs one day before the record date, which is the day on which shareholders need to be on the company's books in order to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is of consequence because whenever a stock is bought or sold, the trade takes at least one business day to settle. Thus, you can purchase Eldorado Gold's shares before the 1st of December in order to receive the dividend, which the company will pay on the 15th of December.

The company's next dividend payment will be US$0.075 per share, on the back of last year when the company paid a total of US$0.30 to shareholders. Calculating the last year's worth of payments shows that Eldorado Gold has a trailing yield of 1.1% on the current share price of CA$40.11. Dividends are an important source of income to many shareholders, but the health of the business is crucial to maintaining those dividends. That's why we should always check whether the dividend payments appear sustainable, and if the company is growing.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Dividends are usually paid out of company profits, so if a company pays out more than it earned then its dividend is usually at greater risk of being cut. Eldorado Gold is paying out just 7.5% of its profit after tax, which is comfortably low and leaves plenty of breathing room in the case of adverse events. Yet cash flows are even more important than profits for assessing a dividend, so we need to see if the company generated enough cash to pay its distribution. Eldorado Gold paid a dividend despite reporting negative free cash flow over the last twelve months. This may be due to heavy investment in the business, but this is still suboptimal from a dividend sustainability perspective.

View our latest analysis for Eldorado Gold

Click here to see the company's payout ratio, plus analyst estimates of its future dividends.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Companies with consistently growing earnings per share generally make the best dividend stocks, as they usually find it easier to grow dividends per share. If earnings decline and the company is forced to cut its dividend, investors could watch the value of their investment go up in smoke. That's why it's comforting to see Eldorado Gold's earnings have been skyrocketing, up 28% per annum for the past five years.

Given that Eldorado Gold has only been paying a dividend for a year, there's not much of a past history to draw insight from.

The Bottom Line

Is Eldorado Gold an attractive dividend stock, or better left on the shelf? We're glad to see the company has been improving its earnings per share while also paying out a low percentage of income. However, it's not great to see it paying out what we see as an uncomfortably high percentage of its cash flow. In summary, while it has some positive characteristics, we're not inclined to race out and buy Eldorado Gold today.

So while Eldorado Gold looks good from a dividend perspective, it's always worthwhile being up to date with the risks involved in this stock. For example - Eldorado Gold has 2 warning signs we think you should be aware of.

data.title: How a Small Potash Developer Jumped A Massive Hurdle in Saskatchewan
data.description:
Key points

  • Buffalo Potash has connected all three horizontal wells underground at its Disley Project in Saskatchewan, proving its patented extraction design works in practice.

  • By showing fluid can reliably move between wells, Buffalo has cleared the prime technical risk that kept it trading at a discount to conventional potash miners.

  • The next step is pumping potash-rich brine to the surface ahead of a targeted Q1 2027 production start, though the project is still advancing without a formal feasibility study.

If you look at the world’s major potash mines, almost all of them belong to the major players like Mosaic (NYSE:MOS) or K+S. That’s not coincidental. Extracting potash traditionally requires sinking vertical wells and billions of dollars in infrastructure. 

That expenditure is typically a barrier to entry that’s kept smaller players on the sidelines. 

Buffalo Potash (TSXV:BUFF) is trying to rewrite the playbook on a prime patch of land in the middle of Saskatchewan. A plot that happens to border Mosaic’s Belle Plaine mine and K+S’ Bethune operation. Instead of drilling straight down with expensive vertical wells, Buffalo opted to lay three 565-meter horizontal wells along the base of the deposit. Essentially, one central injector flanked by two producers. 

Until this week, that exact setup was one of the reasons investors were staying cautious. Using horizontal wells to dissolve potash underground is the new kid on the block. 

Buffalo patented it and dubbed it the “Horizontal Line-Drive” (HLD) method, which has never proven its mettle at this scale. Mostly due to the fact that if the salty water pumped down doesn’t reliably reach the outer wells, the whole model is kaput. 

Question quelled

That question was just answered. Following its first well connection on November 23, Buffalo confirmed on the 25th that it’s connected the second producer well, completing an underground loop across all three wells. They’ve also reported pressure and fluid readings matching the subsurface engineering model predictions.

“Connecting the second producer well gives us confidence that what we're seeing underground is repeatable, which is exactly what we set out to demonstrate at this stage," CEO Steve Halabura said, noting the team is now laser-focused on delivering brine to the surface. 

For the investors 

So, what happens next (and why does it matter)? Simply put, Buffalo has cleared the engineering hurdle that often snags other runners. From here on, the process relies on the same solution-mining principles used across the region for 60 years which is to circulate brine, dissolve the potash and pump the mineral-rich liquid up for processing. 

Before it sees sunlight however, engineers will use an 11-stage packer system. Sounds complicated, but it’s essentially just a series of adjustable internal seals along the wells that pressurize different sections and widen the flow underground. 

This is also known as the Mining Plane.

Disley: by the numbers

Quick note: Economic figures come from Buffalo’s May 2026 Preliminary Economic Assessment. All the details can be found in Buffalo’s November 25 release.

What it all means

For investors, the broader story is the proof in the method’s pudding and how the tech can potentially shift Buffalo’s valuation narrative seeing as horizontal solution mining is designed to deliver lower operating costs and a smaller environmental footprint. 

Successfully proving it works at the Initial Production Module (IPM) gives Buffalo a repeatable, low-CapEx blueprint to build on. 

Once the company hits first production, still targeted for Q1 2027, the IP will be proven for deployment across other spaces at Disley, which can handily lead to scaling to a 1.125 million-metric-ton-per-year target.

What could still go wrong?

There is still plenty of executional risk between an underground connection and commercial cash flow. Buffalo is advancing the starter plant based on assessments rather than formal mineral feasibility reports. This means the real-world recoveries, costs and timelines can still vary wildly. They’re also working to finalize a royalty deal with Altius Royalty Corporation (announced October 22) to fund the remaining site and surface processing build-out. 

This article was written independently by the author, without issuer input or approval. Buffalo Potash has a marketing services agreement with Simply Wall St. Details on compensation and other important information can be found in the disclosure and disclaimer at the end of this narrative.

Technical and scientific information in this article is drawn from Buffalo Potash Corp’s news release dated November 25, 2026, which was reviewed and approved by independent Qualified Person Jared Galenzoski, P.Geo., FIMMM, in accordance with National Instrument 43-101. Readers should note that no mineral reserves have been established at the Disley Project, the company’s decision to advance the Initial Production Module is based on a Preliminary Economic Assessment rather than a feasibility study, and its Horizontal Line-Drive mining method has not yet been operated at commercial scale.

However, the silver lining is that the sale only reduced their total holding by 1.2%, so we're hesitant to read anything much into it, on its own.

Chemung Financial Insider Transactions Over The Last Year

Over the last year, we can see that the biggest insider sale was by the Executive VP & Chief Information Officer, Loren Cole, for US$431k worth of shares, at about US$83.50 per share. So we know that an insider sold shares at around the present share price of US$79.12. While insider selling is a negative, to us, it is more negative if the shares are sold at a lower price. We note that this sale took place at around the current price, so it isn't a major concern, though it's hardly a good sign.

Insider Ownership

Looking at the total insider shareholdings in a company can help to inform your view of whether they are well aligned with common shareholders. Usually, the higher the insider ownership, the more likely it is that insiders will be incentivised to build the company for the long term. It appears that Chemung Financial insiders own 19% of the company, worth about US$71m. We've certainly seen higher levels of insider ownership elsewhere, but these holdings are enough to suggest alignment between insiders and the other shareholders.

So What Does This Data Suggest About Chemung Financial Insiders?

Insiders haven't bought Chemung Financial stock in the last three months, but there was some selling. Looking to the last twelve months, our data doesn't show any insider buying. But since Chemung Financial is profitable and growing, we're not too worried by this. Insider ownership isn't particularly high, so this analysis makes us cautious about the company.
